newsitem.title: UK: BA expects Air Liberte decision late Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: BA expects Air Liberte decision late Tuesday.

text.p: British Airways chief executive Robert Ayling said on Tuesday he expected a decision from a French commercial court later in the day on BA's proposal to take over insolvent airline Air Liberte.
Ayling told reporters at a news conference that the court's decision was expected at 1600 local time and that BA would make a statement after that.
The offer, if agreed, would see BA take a 70 percent stake in Liberte while French bank Rivaud would end up with 30 percent.

No other formal offers have been lodged with Air Liberte's administrator but British entrepreneur Richard Branson's new Belgian-based short-haul airline Virgin Express has said it is trying to put together a late counterbid.

Ayling said on Tuesday that there was a limit to how much BA would pay for the insolvent French airline but he saw it as a prime opportunity to exploit the French domestic market by combining Air Liberte with BA's local subsidiary TAT.
"It will be an opportunity missed if we don't get it but obviously there is a price beyond which we are not going to pay," he told Reuters in an interview.

BA believes it can make the airline profitable by running it in tandem with TAT to give BA critical mass in the French domestic market which will be open to full competition when the European single aviation market comes into force next April.
"We believe that there is a competitive opportunity in France, particularly if you put together the TAT business and the Air Liberte business," Ayling said.
"France has a very large aviation market and it has not yet experienced the impact of the deregulated market which is going to come into full effect in April next year," he said.
"Air Liberte's costs are significantly lower than their competitors and thay have a reputation for service and an enthusiastic young workforce," he added.
On the other hand, Ayling declined to say whether he believed TAT could survive if Air Liberte fell into the hands of a rival.
"If somebody else gets it obviously we will continue to manage our existing (TAT) business there and reflect on the consequences," he said.
"I think we would want to see exactly what happens to the French market overall before thinking about the future and Air Liberte is not the only opportunity.
"That is something I will think about only if we don't pull this (bid for Air Liberte) off," he said.

British Airways and Rivaud announced last month they were offering to pay 780 million francs for the insolvent French regional carrier, comprising 630 million francs for the share capital plus an additional 150 million francs to cover costs incurred by Air Liberte's administrator.
BA, which is to pay 440 million francs for a 70 percent stake plus 100 million of the administration costs, has said it expects to turn the airline back into profit within three years.
Air Liberte lost 650 million francs in the first nine months of 1996.
